events.label: The Amistad captives win their freedom
events.description: Africans illegally trafficked aboard the schooner Amistad rose under Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué), seized the ship, and killed the captain — the most famous of the shipboard revolts that recurred across the whole trade.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Amistad is the most famous successful shipboard revolt, and it came late — 1839, decades after Britain and the US had banned the trade. The Africans aboard had been illegally trafficked to Cuba in defiance of those bans; off the Cuban coast they rose under Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué), seized the schooner, and killed the captain. Shipboard revolt was common across the whole trade — insurers charged extra for the risk and crews carried extra weapons — but it almost always failed against an armed crew. The Amistad is remembered because, this time, the courtroom finished what the rising began (Chapter 9).

events.label: Frederick Douglass gives slavery a witness
events.description: Having escaped slavery in Maryland, Frederick Douglass published his Narrative and became the era's most powerful abolitionist orator and writer — making the case against slavery in his own commanding voice.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most commanding voice of American abolition — an orator of extraordinary power whose best-selling 1845 Narrative made the case in the unanswerable voice of a man who had endured bondage and escaped it. He was so eloquent that pro-slavery skeptics accused him of never having been enslaved at all, which is partly why he named names and places in the book, at real risk to his own freedom. Like Equiano a half-century before (Chapter 7), he insisted that Black people be the agents of their own liberation.

events.label: Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad
events.description: After escaping slavery herself, Harriet Tubman returned repeatedly into the South to lead others north on the Underground Railroad — roughly thirteen trips, some seventy people guided to freedom, never losing one.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tubman escaped slavery and then did something almost beyond belief: she went back, again and again, into slave territory to lead others out. She made roughly thirteen trips and personally guided some seventy people to freedom, never losing a single one, with a bounty on her head. She carried a pistol — as much to steady the frightened as to face slave-catchers — and timed escapes for winter nights and Saturdays, when runaway notices could not be printed until Monday. Later she served as a Union scout and spy, guiding a raid that freed hundreds more.

events.label: The Underground Railroad moves the enslaved north
events.description: A loose, improvised web of safe houses, guides, and free Black and white allies helped enslaved people escape the South toward the northern states and Canada — defying the Fugitive Slave Act that reached even into free territory.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "railroad" was not a railroad and mostly not even organized — it was a loose, dangerous, improvised web of safe houses, secret routes, and free Black and white allies willing to break the law to move people to freedom. It borrowed railway code: "conductors" led escapees, "stations" were safe houses, "passengers" were the people fleeing. Its great enemy was the Fugitive Slave Act, which compelled even Northerners to help capture runaways and pushed many escapees all the way to Canada, beyond the reach of US law. Most of the real work was done quietly, by the escapees themselves and the people who risked everything to hide them.

events.label: Brazil's law ends the transatlantic slave trade
events.description: Under British naval pressure, Brazil's 1850 Eusébio de Queiroz law effectively halted the Atlantic import of captives — the ocean trade's last great destination closing its ports, though slavery within Brazil persisted a generation more.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Brazil was the last great destination of the ocean trade, and it closed its ports only under sustained British naval pressure. The 1850 Eusébio de Queiroz law finally made the Atlantic import of captives effective — earlier bans had been openly ignored, smuggling running briskly — and this time the Royal Navy was prepared to enter Brazilian waters to enforce it. But it ended only the import, not slavery: Brazil would hold enslaved people for another thirty-eight years, dismantling the institution itself in slow, deliberate steps (Chapter 9).

events.label: The Emancipation Proclamation
events.description: Amid the Civil War, Lincoln declared the enslaved in the rebelling Confederate states free — a limited war measure that nonetheless redefined the war as a struggle over slavery and opened the Union Army to nearly 200,000 Black soldiers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Proclamation was a war measure with real limits — it declared free only the enslaved people in the rebelling Confederate states, where the Union could not yet enforce it, and left slavery technically intact in the loyal border states. But it transformed the meaning of the war into a struggle over slavery itself, and it opened the way for nearly 200,000 Black men, many formerly enslaved, to fight in the Union Army for their own people's freedom — which proved decisive to Union victory and made the soldiers themselves agents of emancipation.

events.label: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishes U.S. slavery
events.description: Ratified at the war's end, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery throughout the United States — ending an institution built into the nation since its founding, at the cost of its bloodiest war.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Thirteenth Amendment wrote slavery out of the supreme law of a nation that had been built on it since its founding — the institution finally abolished not by a single legislature's mercy but at the cost of the bloodiest war in American history, some 750,000 dead. The amendment carried one fateful exception: it permits involuntary servitude "as a punishment for crime," a clause whose later use against Black Americans through convict labor became part of slavery's long afterlife. But in 1865 it ended legal slavery across the entire United States.

events.label: Brazil's Law of the Free Womb
events.description: Brazil's 1871 Rio Branco law declared children born to enslaved women free — though only after years of labor for their mother's owner — a gradualist step meant to let slavery die out slowly rather than end at a stroke.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Law of the Free Womb was gradualism by design: children born to enslaved women after 1871 were declared free — but only in name, since they owed their mother's owner years of labor first, typically until age twenty-one. The intent was to let slavery die out slowly as the existing enslaved generation aged, rather than ending it at a stroke. Other partial laws followed, freeing the elderly. Each was a step that let the slaveholding class adjust — and each fell short of the clean abolition that enslaved people were already forcing by deserting the plantations.

events.label: Brazil's Golden Law ends slavery in the Americas
events.description: Princess Isabel signed the Lei Áurea, abolishing slavery in Brazil outright and without compensation — the last country in the Americas to do so, closing nearly four centuries of Atlantic bondage.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Golden Law was three words long in its essential clause and abolished slavery in Brazil outright — with no compensation to slaveholders and no apprenticeship period, a cleaner abolition in that one respect than Britain's or the United States'. By 1888 the institution was already crumbling: enslaved people were deserting the plantations in growing numbers, abolishing slavery with their feet faster than the legislature could on paper. Princess Isabel signed it while her father, the emperor, was abroad. It freed the last legally enslaved people in the Western Hemisphere — and helped cost the monarchy its throne the next year.

events.label: Vodou survives the crossing in Haiti
events.description: Haitian Vodou fused West and Central African religions with Catholicism into a faith centered on the spirits called lwa — a religion that sustained the enslaved and, at Bois Caïman, helped fire their revolution.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Vodou was not a sideshow to Haitian history — it was woven into the revolution itself, with the ceremony at Bois Caïman remembered as its spark (Chapter 8). The faith fused the gods of West and Central Africa (especially the Fon and Yoruba) with Catholicism into a coherent religion centered on a great many spirits called lwa, served through drumming, dance, song, and possession. The popular image of "voodoo" as sinister black magic, complete with dolls and curses, is a racist caricature largely manufactured by outsiders frightened by Haiti's revolution and entertained by Hollywood; the actual religion is communal and life-sustaining.

events.label: Candomblé takes root in Brazil
events.description: Enslaved Africans, especially Yoruba speakers, preserved their orixá worship in Brazil as Candomblé — a faith hidden behind Catholic saints through generations of repression and vibrantly alive today.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Candomblé survived through an act of cultural concealment. Enslaved Yoruba and other West Africans in Brazil were made to become Catholic — so they matched their own deities, the orixás, to Catholic saints and went on worshipping the old powers in plain sight, behind the saints' images. A spirit of iron and war might be honored behind a sword-bearing saint; to the master watching, it looked like Catholic devotion. Built especially around Yoruba worship and carried by the huge numbers brought to Brazil, Candomblé is not a survival on life support but a living religion with millions of adherents today.

events.label: Santería emerges in the Spanish Caribbean
events.description: In Cuba, enslaved Yoruba people reworked their religion into Santería (Regla de Ocha) — masking the orishas behind Catholic saints — another of the diaspora's enduring faiths born of survival under bondage.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Santería is Cuba's version of the same survival — Yoruba worship of the orishas, reworked under bondage and masked behind the Catholic saints, so that the enslaved could keep their gods while appearing to pray to the church's. Its other name, Regla de Ocha, points to its formal lineage of priesthood and initiation. Like Candomblé in Brazil, it was born of concealment and is now a living faith with adherents across Cuba and the diaspora — proof that the gods crossed the Middle Passage with the people who carried them and survived everything done to erase them.

events.label: The Gullah preserve an African coast culture
events.description: On the relatively isolated Sea Islands of South Carolina and Georgia, the Gullah preserved a distinct creole language, African-rooted foodways, and crafts — a piece of West and Central Africa kept alive on American soil.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Gullah are a window onto how much could survive when conditions allowed. Because the Sea Islands of South Carolina and Georgia were relatively isolated — heavily Black, separated from the mainland, left somewhat to themselves between malarial growing seasons — the Gullah retained more of their African inheritance, more directly, than almost any other community in the United States. They speak a distinct creole language preserving African vocabulary and structure; they kept African-rooted foodways (rice at the center), the coiled sweetgrass baskets woven exactly as in West Africa, folktales, songs, and naming practices.

events.label: Reckoning and reparations
events.description: Long after abolition, the descendants of the enslaved have pressed for acknowledgment and material repair — a demand rooted in the stark fact that when slavery ended, it was usually the enslavers, not the enslaved, who were paid.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: When slavery ended, it was usually the enslavers who were compensated, not the enslaved — Britain paid its slaveholders £20 million in 1833 and the freed nothing; France forced Haiti to pay reparations to the very slaveholders it had defeated (Chapter 8). The case for repair rests on that asymmetry: the people who were stolen, sold, and worked for free were released into poverty and new systems of discrimination, while the wealth their labor created stayed where it was. The question is alive today — debated in parliaments, universities, and international bodies, as banks, insurers, churches, and governments begin to investigate their own historical roles.

events.label: Sugarcane: the crop that drove the trade
events.description: Sugar was the engine of the Atlantic system — wildly profitable, brutally labor-hungry, and so lethal to grow that it consumed enslaved lives faster than any other crop.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sugar was the engine, and it was an engine that burned people. The cane has to be cut by hand in blazing heat, hauled to the mill before the juice spoils, then crushed and boiled around the clock during harvest, in heat and danger that wrecked bodies. No free person would do it willingly, which is exactly why the crop and slavery fused. Medieval Europe had known sugar only as a rare luxury for the very rich; once it could be grown at scale by enslaved labor, it flooded the market, reshaped European diets, and made fortunes worth killing for.

events.label: Coffee opens a second plantation frontier
events.description: Coffee cultivation, above all in Saint-Domingue and later Brazil, opened a second plantation frontier in the cooler highlands — doubling the demand for enslaved labor and extending the system into new land.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Coffee opened a second plantation frontier in the eighteenth century, climbing into the cooler highlands where sugar would not grow. In Saint-Domingue the coffee estates spread across the mountains above the cane plains, and the colony became the world's largest coffee producer as well as its largest sugar producer — doubling the demand for enslaved labor on a single island. Later the frontier moved to the hills of Brazil, where coffee would outlast slavery itself and become the country's defining crop. Each new crop was a new reason to buy more people.

events.label: Cap-Français: the jewel of the French Caribbean
events.description: Cap-Français, the 'Paris of the Antilles,' was Saint-Domingue's glittering capital — a showcase of European wealth built entirely on slave-grown sugar, and later a battleground of the Haitian Revolution.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Cap-Français was called the "Paris of the Antilles" — a glittering port city of theaters, fine houses, and merchant wealth, the showcase of the richest colony on earth, all of it built on slave-grown sugar. It became a battleground of the revolution and was burned more than once in the fighting. The contrast is the colony in miniature: European elegance on the surface, a half-million enslaved people dying to pay for it underneath. The city survives today as Cap-Haïtien, Haiti's second city.

events.label: Charleston: North America's great slaving port
events.description: Charleston was the largest port of entry for enslaved Africans in mainland British North America, its wealth built on lowcountry rice and indigo — with nearby Sullivan's Island the point of arrival for a great share of them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Charleston was the largest port of entry for enslaved Africans in mainland British North America — a substantial share of all the captives brought to what became the United States passed through it. Many were quarantined first on Sullivan's Island, sometimes called the "Ellis Island of Black America" for the role it played as a point of arrival. The city's wealth and refined society were built on the rice and indigo grown in the surrounding lowcountry, and on the captives — prized for their West African rice knowledge (Chapter 5) — who were sold from its wharves.

events.label: Nantes: France's slaving capital
events.description: The Atlantic port of Nantes outfitted the largest share of French slave ships, its merchant elite growing rich on a trade the city now memorializes openly on its quays.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Nantes outfitted the largest share of French slave ships — by many counts roughly half of the entire French trade passed through it. The wealth built the grand townhouses of its merchant elite along the Loire. In 1998 Nantes became one of the first European port cities to formally confront that past, and it later opened a major Memorial to the Abolition of Slavery on its quays — a public reckoning with a fortune the city had long preferred not to discuss.

events.label: The House of Slaves on Gorée
events.description: Gorée's House of Slaves, with its 'Door of No Return,' became the trade's most visited memorial — a place of pilgrimage and mourning, whatever historians conclude about its exact historical traffic.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The House of Slaves and its "Door of No Return" are the emotional heart of the trade's memory — visited by popes, presidents, and pilgrims of the African diaspora, who stand at the doorway opening onto the ocean where ships once waited. Historians caution that the volume of captives through this specific building was probably modest and its layout partly memorial rather than purely functional. None of that diminishes its meaning: it is a place built for mourning and remembrance, and it does that work whatever its exact eighteenth-century traffic.

events.label: Pan-Africanism answers the diaspora's scattering
events.description: Out of the trade's forced dispersal grew Pan-Africanism — the movement, built across a series of congresses, to reunite and uplift people of African descent worldwide against racism and colonialism.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Pan-Africanism was, in a real sense, a political answer to the trade's central act — the forced dispersal of Africans across the world. Emerging around the turn of the twentieth century, it held that people of African descent everywhere shared a common heritage and cause and should unite against racism and colonialism. A series of Pan-African Congresses, drawing figures like W. E. B. Du Bois, built the framework; it shaped anti-colonial movements across Africa and civil-rights struggles across the Americas. If the trade had scattered a people, Pan-Africanism sought to reunite them in spirit and purpose.

events.label: The demographics of a four-century atrocity
events.description: Scholars reconstructing the trade voyage by voyage count roughly 12.5 million Africans embarked and 10.7 million landed across some 36,000 documented voyages — the best estimates the evidence supports, and almost certainly a floor.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: These are the numbers everything else rests on, and getting them right is a duty. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database reconstructed the trade voyage by voyage from surviving shipping records — some 36,000 documented voyages — to reach roughly 12.5 million Africans embarked and roughly 10.7 million who survived to land, the difference of about 1.8 million dying on the crossing. They are the best estimates the evidence supports, and almost certainly a floor, not a ceiling: not every voyage left a record, and the figures do not count those killed in the raids and the march to the coast before any ship.

events.label: The Oyo Empire and the Yoruba supply
events.description: The cavalry-powered Oyo Empire dominated the Yoruba lands and the Slave Coast hinterland, channeling captives toward the Bight of Benin — and, in its later collapse, sending the Yoruba whose culture shaped Brazil and Cuba.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Oyo's distinctive weapon was cavalry — unusual in West Africa, where the tsetse fly, whose bite carries a disease lethal to horses, confined cavalry to the drier northern fringes. Oyo sat far enough north to keep mounted armies, and used them to dominate the Yoruba lands and channel captives toward the busy ports of the Bight of Benin. When Oyo later collapsed in the early nineteenth century, its wars threw huge numbers of Yoruba people into the trade — which is why Yoruba religion and culture left so deep a mark in Brazil and Cuba (Chapter 10).

events.label: The Kingdom of Loango on the Central African coast
events.description: North of the Kongo, the independent Kingdom of Loango funneled captives from its hinterland to Dutch, English, and French traders — a reminder that Central Africa, not just West Africa, was a heartland of the trade.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Loango is the reminder that the Central African coast, not just West Africa, was a heartland of the trade. North of the Kongo, this independent African kingdom channeled captives from its interior to Dutch, English, and French traders, and it did so on its own terms — controlling access, setting customs, and dealing as a sovereign power rather than a subject one. Its quieter role complicates the familiar map: enormous numbers of the people carried across the Atlantic came not from West Africa at all, but from this central stretch of the continent.

events.label: Britain's West India Interest defends slavery
events.description: The West India Interest — a powerful lobby of Caribbean planters, merchants, and bankers — fought abolition in Parliament for decades, a measure of how deeply slavery's profits ran through respectable British politics.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Abolition was hard because you were not fighting a few villains but a whole economy. The West India Interest — the lobby of Caribbean planters and the merchants and bankers tied to them — was one of the most powerful blocs in British politics, with members of Parliament, newspapers, and vast wealth at its command. For decades it fought every abolition bill, warning that ending the trade would ruin the colonies, wreck the economy, and simply hand the business to France. Its long resistance is the measure of how deeply slavery's profits ran through respectable British life.

events.label: Bristol's fortune from the trade
events.description: Before Liverpool eclipsed it, Bristol was a leading British slaving port, its merchants and civic institutions enriched by the commerce in human beings — a legacy the city still openly argues over today.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before Liverpool eclipsed it, Bristol had its own slaving boom, and the wealth sank deep into the city's civic fabric — its merchant elite, its grand buildings, its charities. Edward Colston, a leading Royal African Company official whose money endowed Bristol institutions for centuries, became the most contested symbol of that legacy: his statue was pulled down and thrown into the harbor in 2020. The reckoning over Bristol's slaving past is a live argument precisely because the profits never fully left the city.

events.label: Indentured servitude on the road to slavery
events.description: Early English colonies leaned on indentured servants — Europeans bound for a fixed term — before the law hardened labor into lifelong, hereditary racial slavery, closing the door that some early Africans had once passed through to freedom.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: For a few early decades the line between bound labor and slavery was not yet sharp. Many of Virginia's first laborers were European indentured servants — poor people who sold years of their labor in exchange for passage across the ocean — and some early Africans, too, served terms and gained freedom and even property. Then the colonies wrote that flexibility out of existence: a poor white servant served his term and went free, while an African and all his descendants were enslaved forever. Indentured servitude was the older world that racial slavery hardened out of.

events.label: The Mascarene trade and the Indian Ocean parallel
events.description: On the Mascarene Islands of the Indian Ocean, the French ran sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans and Malagasy — a reminder that the Atlantic's lethal island-sugar formula had cousins worldwide.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Mascarene Islands — Mauritius and Réunion in the Indian Ocean — are a reminder that Atlantic-style plantation slavery had cousins worldwide. There the French ran sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans and Malagasy from nearby Madagascar, drawing on a separate Indian Ocean slave trade that ran alongside the Atlantic one. The comparison cuts against any notion that the Atlantic system was a lone aberration: the same lethal formula — islands, sugar, and people bought to be worked to death — was being applied on the far side of the world at the same time.

events.label: Saint-Louis: France's Senegal foothold
events.description: The island town of Saint-Louis at the mouth of the Senegal River was France's chief West African base, organizing the gum and slave trades — and home to the powerful signares, African and mixed-race women traders.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Saint-Louis, on an island at the mouth of the Senegal River, was France's chief West African base — the hub of its trade in gum arabic and in captives along the Upper Guinea coast. It became home to a distinctive community of signares, African and mixed-race women traders who married European men, accumulated property and enslaved people of their own, and wielded real commercial power in the town. Saint-Louis is another reminder that the coast was a world of brokers and intermediaries, not a simple line between European buyers and African sellers.

events.label: Atlantic Creoles bridge two worlds
events.description: On the African coast and in the early Americas, Atlantic Creoles — people of mixed African and European heritage and culture — brokered the trade, interpreted, and moved between societies the way no one else could.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Atlantic Creoles show that the coast was not a simple wall with Africans on one side and Europeans on the other. Born in the trading posts and port towns, of mixed African and European descent and culture, they spoke several languages, often held Christian and African beliefs at once, and made their living as the brokers, interpreters, and middlemen the trade could not run without. Some were the children of European traders and African women; some were Africans who had learned European ways. They are the human seam of the Atlantic world — and their identities would flower, in the Americas, into the creole cultures of Chapter 10.

events.label: The Bight of Benin's Slave Coast
events.description: The stretch of the Bight of Benin known bluntly as the 'Slave Coast,' centered on ports like Ouidah and Lagos, shipped enormous numbers of captives — one of a row of West African shores that European maps named for their chief export.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "Slave Coast" was named, baldly, for its main export. This stretch of the Bight of Benin — centered on ports like Ouidah and Lagos — shipped enormous numbers of captives, fed by the wars of inland powers like Dahomey and Oyo (Chapter 3). The naming itself is worth pausing on: European maps labeled West Africa's shores by their chief trade goods — the Gold Coast, the Ivory Coast, the Grain (or Pepper) Coast — and one whole stretch was simply the coast where the trade good was people. The casual geography of it captures how ordinary the traffic had become.

events.label: The slave auction and the 'scramble'
events.description: On arrival, captives were sold at public auction or in chaotic 'scrambles' — buyers rushing en masse to grab people at a fixed price — sales that completed the reduction to property and routinely tore families apart.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "scramble" was its own distinct horror, remembered by survivors with particular dread. Instead of a one-by-one auction, a fixed price was set in advance, and at a signal the waiting buyers rushed in a mob into the pen to grab and claim as many people as they could lay hands on. To captives who could not understand a word being said, did not know where they were, and had just survived the crossing, it was bedlam — strangers seizing them in a scrum. Either method, auction or scramble, completed the transformation into property and routinely shattered the bonds that had survived the ship.

events.label: Pirates prey on the slaving lanes
events.description: Pirates like Bartholomew Roberts raided the West African slaving coast and its shipping — a violent sideshow that preyed on the same Atlantic commerce it sometimes plundered, and occasionally plundered slave ships themselves.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Piracy was a violent sideshow that fed on the same Atlantic commerce as the trade. Captains like Bartholomew Roberts — "Black Bart," among the most successful pirates of the era — raided the West African slaving coast and its shipping, sometimes seizing slave ships outright. The relationship was parasitic and tangled: pirates preyed on slavers, occasionally freed or recruited captives, and just as often simply sold them on themselves. The slaving lanes, dense with valuable cargo and far from naval protection, were exactly the hunting grounds the great pirates of the early eighteenth century preferred.

events.label: Négritude reclaims a diasporic identity
events.description: Writers across the French-speaking Black world launched Négritude — among them Aimé Césaire and Léopold Sédar Senghor — a literary and political movement that reclaimed African heritage with pride against centuries of dehumanization.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Négritude took the very identity the trade had tried to degrade and reclaimed it with pride. Launched in 1930s Paris by Black writers from the French-speaking world — among them Aimé Césaire of Martinique and Léopold Sédar Senghor, later the first president of Senegal — it insisted that African heritage, sensibility, and civilization had profound value, against a colonial order that taught the opposite. The movement's name itself, taking a word that had been an insult and wearing it as a banner, was a deliberate act of reversal — the descendants of the enslaved making the case for their full humanity in the language of their former masters.

events.label: Trans-Saharan slavery, the older trade
events.description: Long before and alongside the Atlantic system, the older trans-Saharan slave trade carried captives north across the desert — vast in its own right, but slower, differently shaped, and never reaching the Atlantic trade's industrial scale.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The trans-Saharan trade had carried enslaved Africans north across the desert for roughly a thousand years before the first Portuguese caravel arrived, and it did not stop when the Atlantic trade began — the two ran side by side for centuries. But they differed in shape: the Saharan trade moved people more slowly and took a higher share of women and children, often into domestic roles, while the Atlantic trade, hungry for field labor, took mostly young men and reached an industrial concentration — millions in a few generations — that was new in the world. The comparison is context, not equivalence, and not an excuse.
